newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Ireland turns up heat at IGC.
newsitem.headline: Ireland turns up heat at IGC.

text.p: Ireland risked the displeasure of its European Union partners on Tuesday, seeking to put pace into the inter-governmental conference (IGC) by asking countries to say when they will accept Qualified Majority Voting.

At the end of a two day negotiating session, the EU president said it had handed its partners a questionnaire asking in just what circumstances they would be willing to give up unanimity in favour of QMV.
"Obviously we would like delegations to respond (to the questionnaire), say within the next week or so," Noel Dorr, Irish chairman of the IGC's main negotiating group, said.
Ireland is under pressure to speed up the IGC negotiations -- which began formally in March -- in order to have a draft treaty ready by for an EU summit in December.
A special EU summit, designed to give the IGC a push, is also to be held in Dublin on October 5.

But despite the widespread calls for the talks to be speeded up, officials and diplomats said a number of countries were reluctant to take a stand at what they say is an early stage in the negotiations.
"If the past two IGCs are anything to go by, there will be a mad rush at the end," said one diplomat.
Most officials said they expected countries would eventually fill out the questionnaire, but that some countries had no idea at this stage what they could accept.
Dorr said the questionnaire was informal and did not tie any country to any position.
"We have emphasised that it is not a major document. It simply stops us from going around and asking (in each specific case," he said.
France, Germany, the European Commission and a number of other EU players have been urging progress in the talks, but officials said the differences in the bloc remain vivid.

Dorr said the questionnaire itself reflected the divisions. There was no consensus on an overall criterion for deciding when something should be taken by QMV, so the negotiators needed to look at the issue on a case-by-case basis.
Similarly, he said, the negotiators had failed to agree on overall criteria for extending co-decision for the European Parliament.
This had meant that the negotiators had to use a European Commission proposal as a basis, again, for a case-by-case study of the issue.
"No clear approach emerged, so we focused on the Commission paper," Dorr said.
In other institutional matters, the negotiators remained divided on how many European commissioners there should be in an enlarged Union.

Dorr said that while some large countries believed that having one commissioner per country in a larger bloc was an invitation to inefficency, smaller countries believed that having a commissioner was a way of guaranteeing them a voice.
"The balance seems to be on the side of the smaller countries," Dorr said.
The meeting of foreign ministers' representatives on Monday and Tuesday had also discussed the European Court fo Justice and the role of national parliaments, he said.
The negotiators had had an informal lunch with the president of the court.
No decisions were close on the Court, but discussion among negotiators had included questions about whether there should be a series of lower courts or an appeals body.
There were some concerns, Door said, about having too many judges on the court, thereby turning it into a debating chamber.
Some countries had agreed to study British proposals for changing the court, he said. Britain wants to give the court certain powers allowing it to limit the retroactive aspects of its rulings.
On the role of national parliaments, Dorr said there was some pressure for more coordination with assemblies, but that there was no call for a new body to be created.
